\chapter*{Abstract}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Abstract}

Mutual information (MI) measures how much knowing one variable reduces
uncertainty about another. This thesis develops a test for comparing MI
between two categorical variables across independent populations. The
Normal Wald test uses a normal approximation for this comparison, which
can give inaccurate false-positive rates when samples are small or contain
many rare category combinations.

The proposed Expanded Welch--Satterthwaite test (Expanded Welch) retains
Wald's estimated MI difference and standard error but compares the test
statistic with a Student \(t\) distribution. To choose its degrees of
freedom, the thesis derives a first-order approximation to how much the
variance estimate within that standard error changes between samples.
The calculation accounts for changes in cell probabilities and their row
and column totals.

Simulations assess the approximations and compare false-positive rates
and power to detect genuine MI differences. Near independence, sampling
noise can make the degrees-of-freedom approximations inaccurate. An
online-shopping application illustrates the tests on observed data.

Expanded Welch brings false-positive rates closer to 5\% in selected
small-sample settings, with lower power under the usual rejection
thresholds. We also adjust the rejection thresholds to give both tests
approximately 5\% false positives at a chosen common MI value. Expanded
Welch then has higher power in some comparisons, but this advantage can
reverse when a different common MI value is used for the adjustment.
Changing the rejection threshold cannot correct bias in the MI difference
or errors in its estimated uncertainty.

\chapter{Introduction}
\label{chap:introduction}

Mutual information (MI) measures the average reduction in uncertainty about
one variable obtained by observing another \citep{bossomaier2016}.
For example, a categorical input feature
\(X\) may carry different amounts of information about a class label \(Y\) in two
populations. This thesis develops and evaluates a statistical test
for that comparison using two independently collected samples.

In practice, MI is estimated from observed data. Two samples can produce
different MI estimates even when the population MI values are equal,
because their observed counts vary from sample to sample. A statistical
test must account for this sampling variation before an estimated
difference can be interpreted as evidence of a population difference.
\section{Why the comparison is difficult}

The Normal Wald test \citep{wald1943,vanderVaart1998} divides the estimated
MI difference by its standard error and compares the resulting statistic
with a standard normal distribution. At a 5\% significance level, the
intended false-positive rate is 5\% when the population MI values are
equal. The normal
approximation can be inaccurate in small or sparse samples, causing the
test to reject equal MI too often or too rarely.

Both the MI difference and its standard error are estimated from count
tables, whose cells record how often each pair of categories occurs.
MI depends on the cell probabilities and their row and column totals.
When samples are small and rare combinations of categories occur only a
few times or not at all, the resulting probability estimates can distort
both the MI difference and its estimated uncertainty.

The proposed Expanded Welch--Satterthwaite test (Expanded Welch) retains
Wald's estimated MI difference and standard error but uses a Student
\(t\) distribution instead of the standard normal distribution. Choosing
its degrees of freedom requires estimating how much the MI variance
estimates change from sample to sample. For MI, this calculation must
account for the fact that changing a cell probability also changes its
row and column totals and the MI values calculated from them. This thesis
derives how these probability changes affect the estimated MI variance
and uses that calculation to obtain degrees of freedom for Expanded Welch.

The Student \(t\) distribution gives Expanded Welch a larger rejection
cutoff than Normal Wald, so it rejects less often. This can reduce false
positives, but it can also reduce statistical power: the probability of
rejecting equal MI when the population MI values genuinely differ.
The evaluation measures the resulting false-positive rates and nominal
power, then compares power after matching rejection at specified equal-MI
populations through independent simulation. Changing the calibration
population checks whether the resulting power comparison is stable.
The frequency of usable p-values is reported alongside these rates.

\section{Research questions}
\label{sec:research-questions}

The thesis addresses two research questions:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{RQ\arabic*:},leftmargin=*]
 \item How accurately do the derived approximations predict the mean and
 sampling variance of the estimated MI variance, and what degrees of
 freedom do they imply near and away from independence?
 \item How do Expanded Welch's false-positive rates and power compare
 with Normal Wald?
 \begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{RQ2.\arabic*:},leftmargin=*,nosep]
  \item How do their false-positive rates compare under equal population MI?
  \item How do their nominal and calibrated power compare when population MI differs?
 \end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
\section{Contributions to the field}

\item \begin{samepage}\textbf{Methodological contribution.} Expanded Welch uses this
  variance sensitivity to choose the degrees of freedom for a two-sample
  test using a Student \(t\) distribution.
  \par
  \end{samepage}

\item \begin{samepage}\textbf{Empirical contribution.} Controlled simulations check
  the variance approximations and compare false-positive rates, power and
  usable results as sample size, table size, category frequencies and MI
  change. A supporting comparison checks whether sparse-table failures
  persist under another association construction.
  \par
  \end{samepage}

\item \textbf{Practical contribution.} The evaluation identifies
  selected populations at common MI 0.02 nats where Expanded Welch brings
  false-positive rates closer to 5\% than Normal Wald, the dependence of calibrated power on
  the fitting population, and estimation errors that make both tests
  unreliable.
\end{enumerate}
\section{Scope and organisation}

The scope of this thesis is the comparison of MI between two populations
using categorical data. Each sample is summarised in a count table, and
both tables use the same fixed row and column categories. The two samples
are independent, and observations within each sample are also independent.
For the main derivation, both populations are assumed to have positive MI
and a positive probability in every cell. The case of zero MI, where
\(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, is considered separately.
The main simulations compare Normal Wald and Expanded Welch using
two-sided tests at the 5\% significance level.

Chapter~\ref{chap:background} reviews the background and literature.
Chapters~\ref{chap:baselines} and~\ref{chap:expanded} define the statistic
and derive Expanded Welch. Chapters~\ref{chap:design} and~\ref{chap:results}
present the experiment, results and online-shopping application.
Chapter~\ref{chap:conclusion} brings together the findings, limitations
and future work. The appendices give supporting calculations,
experimental settings and additional results.

\chapter{Background and Literature Review}
\label{chap:background}

Testing for equal MI in two populations requires an estimate from each
sample and its sampling variance. This chapter develops the MI estimator,
derives its variance and reviews tests for equal population MI.
\section{Information-theoretic foundations}
\subsection{Entropy and information content}

For a discrete random variable \(X\) with probability mass function
\(p_X(x)\), the information content of outcome \(x\) is
\(-\log p_X(x)\).
Rare outcomes have larger information content because they are less expected.
Using natural logarithms gives information in nats. The Shannon entropy is the
expected information content,
\begin{equation}
  H(X)=-\sum_x p_X(x)\log p_X(x).
  \label{eq:entropy}
\end{equation}
Entropy summarises the uncertainty of one random variable before its value is
observed \citep{shannon1948}.

For a pair \((X,Y)\), the joint entropy \(H(X,Y)\) is defined from the joint
probabilities in the same way. The conditional entropy
\(
H(X\mid Y)=H(X,Y)-H(Y)
\)
measures the uncertainty remaining in \(X\) after observing \(Y\).
\subsection{Pointwise and average mutual information}

Because \(P\) is the joint distribution of \((X,Y)\), we also write
\(I(P)\) as \(I(X;Y)\). Its entropy form is
\begin{equation}
  I(X;Y)=H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y).
  \label{eq:mi-entropy-form}
\end{equation}
MI is therefore the average reduction in uncertainty about \(X\) obtained
by observing \(Y\), or equivalently about \(Y\) obtained by observing \(X\).
It is nonnegative and equals zero exactly when
\(p_{ij}=p_{i+}p_{+j}\) for every cell, including zero-probability cells
\citep{bossomaier2016}.

Although MI measures the overall departure from independence, it does not
specify the shape of association. Two populations can have the same MI while assigning
probability to different cells, having different margins, or exhibiting
different association patterns. Equality of MI is therefore weaker than
equality of distributions. The null hypothesis requires equal MI, not
identical cell probabilities in the two population tables.

The logarithm base determines the reporting unit. This thesis uses natural
logarithms, so MI is measured in nats; dividing by \(\log 2\) converts to bits.
This conversion rescales MI and its standard error together but leaves the
degrees of freedom unchanged, so the test result is identical in either unit.

\section{Estimating discrete mutual information}
\label{sec:background-mi-bias}

Under multinomial sampling, the cell counts vary between samples but must
sum to \(n\). An extra observation in one cell therefore leaves fewer
observations for the others. For a fixed set of categories, the plug-in
estimate approaches population MI as the sample grows, but its finite-sample
bias and sampling variance depend on the complete probability table. In particular,
rare cells can change both even when the categories and sample size are
unchanged
\citep{paninski2003}.

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{Estimation beyond the leading bias correction.}

Data are undersampled when too few observations are available to estimate
the joint probabilities reliably. Rare category combinations can then be
poorly represented or absent from the sample. \citet{panzeri1996} derive
analytical bias corrections that account
for the categories with nonzero population probability, but these remain
large-sample approximations. \citet{paninski2003} shows that substantial
error can remain after standard corrections, including the jackknife,
when many categories are poorly sampled. \citet{chaoshen2003} instead
adjust entropy for categories missing from the sample. Their method uses
sample coverage, the total population probability of the categories that
have been observed, and accounts for the different probabilities of
discovering common and rare categories.

Bayesian estimators model the unknown probabilities rather than treating
observed proportions as the complete population.
\citet{nemenman2002} combine priors, or probability weights on possible
populations, to avoid favouring a narrow range of entropy values before
observing the data. This is the Nemenman--Shafee--Bialek (NSB) estimator.
More recently, \citet{piga2024} estimate the strength of a Dirichlet prior
from the observed counts. This strength controls how much the probability
estimates are drawn towards a uniform distribution, including for
unobserved categories.

Entropy estimators can also be combined to estimate MI through
\(I(X;Y)=H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y)\), as in
Equation~\eqref{eq:mi-entropy-form}. \citet{archer2013} study this route
alongside estimators that model the joint probabilities directly. Combining
three separately constructed Bayesian entropy estimates need not correspond
to one joint probability model and can produce negative MI estimates.
Nevertheless, these combined estimators generally outperform the authors'
fully Bayesian MI estimator in their tested examples.

The sampling pattern can also suggest a more targeted estimator.
\citet{hernandez2019} consider a well-sampled, low-entropy variable paired
with a variable whose many categories are poorly sampled. They use the
well-estimated marginal and model the conditional probabilities to estimate
MI, rather than estimating three entropies separately. Their results also
show that combining Bayesian entropy estimates can retain bias under severe
undersampling. Estimation errors need not cancel when MI estimates from
two distinct populations are subtracted. The two-sample problem therefore
requires both a small bias in the estimated difference and a standard error
that describes its sampling variation.

Two MI estimates can differ even when their population values are equal,
because each estimate varies between samples. Testing their difference
therefore requires a standard error that accounts for this sampling
variation. We first derive the established large-sample approximation
for the variance of one plug-in MI estimate:
\begin{equation}
  \Var\{\Ihat(P)\}\approx\frac{V(P)}{n}.
  \label{eq:first-order-mi-var-background}
\end{equation}
Here \(V(P)\), defined below, measures how much the contribution of one
observation varies across the population. The derivation assumes that the
population cell probabilities are positive, so the logarithms and their
derivatives are well defined. This first-order variance is established for
histogram and discrete MI \citep{moddemeijer1989,brillinger2004}.
Section~\ref{sec:welch-background} then explains how this result supports
a comparison between two populations.

The argument proceeds in three steps. First, sampling changes the empirical
cell probabilities. Second, a first-order Taylor expansion translates those
probability errors into an MI error. Third, that error can be written as a
sample average, whose variance is straightforward to calculate.

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{Step 1: From probability errors to MI error.}

Applying this expansion to the three sums in
Equation~\eqref{eq:mi-probability-sums} gives
\begin{align}
  \Ihat(P)-I(P)
  &\approx
  \sum_{i,j}(\log p_{ij}+1)(\widehat p_{ij}-p_{ij})
  \notag\\
  &\quad
  -\sum_i(\log p_{i+}+1)(\widehat p_{i+}-p_{i+})
  \notag\\
  &\quad
  -\sum_j(\log p_{+j}+1)(\widehat p_{+j}-p_{+j}).
  \label{eq:mi-first-order-three-sums}
\end{align}
The margin errors are sums of the corresponding cell errors:
\begin{equation}
  \widehat p_{i+}-p_{i+}
  =\sum_j(\widehat p_{ij}-p_{ij}),
  \qquad
  \widehat p_{+j}-p_{+j}
  =\sum_i(\widehat p_{ij}-p_{ij}).
  \label{eq:margin-errors-from-cells}
\end{equation}
For example, the row-margin sum can now be written as
\begin{align}
  \sum_i(\log p_{i+}+1)(\widehat p_{i+}-p_{i+})
  &=\sum_i\left[
    (\log p_{i+}+1)
    \left\{\sum_j(\widehat p_{ij}-p_{ij})\right\}
    \right]
  \notag\\
  &=\sum_{i,j}(\log p_{i+}+1)(\widehat p_{ij}-p_{ij}).
\end{align}
The inner sum over \(j\) is the probability error for a fixed row \(i\). It
is multiplied by that row's coefficient \(\log p_{i+}+1\); the outer sum then
adds these products over all rows. The column-margin sum can be rearranged in
the same way.

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{Step 2: From cell errors to observation-level errors.}

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{Step 3: Calculate the sampling variance.}

At exact independence, \(p_{ij}=p_{i+}p_{+j}\), so
\(\pmi_P(i,j)=\log 1=0\) in every cell. Hence \(I(P)=0\), \(V(P)=0\), and the
first-order average in Equation~\eqref{eq:mi-error-as-average-background}
vanishes.
A finite sample can still have positive MI. Its leading variation comes from
the squared cell-probability errors in a second-order Taylor expansion, which
produces the usual chi-squared limiting distribution
\citep{brillinger2004,marinescu2025}. Testing independence therefore uses a
chi-squared distribution rather than the normal approximation for comparing
positive MI values.

The preceding section describes the sampling variation of one MI estimate.
For two independent samples, their variance contributions add, providing
the standard error needed to compare their MI estimates. This section
reviews the Normal Wald test, the Welch--Satterthwaite principle and other
approaches to that comparison. The hypothesis is that the populations
have the same MI, \(I(P)=I(Q)\), even when their cell probabilities differ.
\thesisminiheading{The Normal Wald test.}

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{The Welch--Satterthwaite principle.}

The denominator of the statistic contains one estimated variance contribution
from each sample. Under normal sampling, their component degrees of freedom
are \(n_P-1\) and \(n_Q-1\). If \(s_P^2/n_P\) dominates, the formula makes the
combined \(\nu\) close to \(n_P-1\); when both contributions matter, both
samples' degrees of freedom affect \(\nu\). Satterthwaite obtains this form
by matching the mean and variance of their sum to a scaled chi-squared variable
\citep{satterthwaite1946}.

Figure~\ref{fig:normal-student-t} shows that the Student \(t\) distribution
has heavier tails than the standard normal distribution, especially when
\(\nu\) is small. More probability in the tails means a larger absolute
statistic is needed to reject the null at the same significance level.
As \(\nu\) increases, the Student \(t\) distribution approaches the
standard normal distribution, and their rejection cutoffs become closer.

For MI, the estimated variance contributions are \(\Vhat(P)/n_P\) and
\(\Vhat(Q)/n_Q\). The ordinary \(n_P-1\) and \(n_Q-1\) values follow
from the scaled chi-squared distribution of a sample variance under normal
sampling; they do not automatically apply to an estimated MI variance.
Chapter~\ref{chap:expanded} therefore derives the component degrees of
freedom from the sampling variability of \(\Vhat(P)\) and \(\Vhat(Q)\),
using the same moment-matching principle.

This distinction matters because the size of a variance estimate and its
stability answer different questions. The estimate \(\Vhat(P)/n_P\)
describes the expected spread of an MI estimate across samples. The
variability of \(\Vhat(P)\) describes how much that assessment of spread
itself changes across samples. Two variance estimators with the same mean
can have different variability. Satterthwaite's calculation uses both
moments: greater variability relative to the squared mean gives fewer
degrees of freedom and a larger rejection cutoff
\citep{satterthwaite1946}. A sample-size assignment alone does not adapt
to differences in this relative variability between probability tables.

The same principle has been used in regression to account for
uncertainty in estimated variances
\citep{panwall2002,bell2002,kauermann2001,fay2001,imbens2016}.
For example, \citet{panwall2002} calculate approximate degrees of freedom
by examining how a regression variance estimate varies between samples,
and Expanded Welch uses the variability of the estimated MI variance to choose
degrees of freedom in the same way.
These regression precedents address variance estimates that are too small
or confidence intervals that cover too rarely
\citep{bell2002,kauermann2001}. A larger cutoff from the Student \(t\)
distribution can widen the intervals and reduce excessive rejection in such
settings.

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{Previous work on MI uncertainty and comparisons.}

\citet{roulston1999} derives entropy and MI error estimates
using error propagation and examines them numerically. These calculations
describe the uncertainty of an individual estimate, a necessary input to a
comparison of two estimates.
The first-order results of \citet{moddemeijer1989} and
\citet{brillinger2004} give this uncertainty as \(V(P)/n_P\), with
\(V(P)\) determined by the population table. Replacing its probabilities
by observed proportions produces the variance estimate used by Wald.
This supplies a standard error for the MI difference. Choosing a
Welch--Satterthwaite cutoff requires one further quantity: how much the
estimated variance varies when a new sample produces a different table.

A Bayesian approach describes uncertainty about population MI given an
observed table. \citet{hutter2002} and \citet{hutterzaffalon2005} model the
unknown cell probabilities to calculate the variance and shape of the
resulting MI distribution. Our repeated-sampling comparison instead asks
how often Normal Wald and Expanded Welch reject equal MI when new samples
are drawn from fixed populations \(P\) and \(Q\).

The entropy comparison establishes that a Student \(t\) distribution can
be used to compare estimated information quantities, but MI requires
more than substituting a different numerator. MI combines the row,
column and joint entropies of the same observations. Their estimation
errors are connected, because one cell count contributes to all three.
The MI variance formulas in Section~\ref{sec:first-order-mi-background}
account for that connection. Expanded Welch also tracks how the estimated
MI variance changes: a cell change alters
both the weights and the pointwise-MI values whose weighted variance is
being estimated. Thus Hutcheson supplies a close comparison framework,
while the cell and margin derivatives supply the MI-specific inputs.

In a segregation application, \citet{mora2009} derive a normal approximation
for comparing positive population MI between populations and time periods,
providing a direct precedent for the Normal Wald baseline. Their later
peer-reviewed account places the MI index within the segregation literature
\citep{mora2011}.

By contrast, \citet{guha2014} test whether two continuous distributions are identical
using MI between pooled observations and their sample labels.
For discrete data, \citet{drake2014} develop an MI-based \(k\)-sample test
for equality of distributions. These tests compare complete distributions,
not the MI of two variables within each population.

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{Resampling alternatives.}

A bootstrap approximates sampling variation by repeatedly drawing samples
with replacement from the observed data \citep{efron1979}. For this
comparison, samples would be drawn separately from the two observed tables,
using their original sample sizes, and the MI difference recalculated for
each pair. Resampling from separate empirical probability tables allows
their cell probabilities to differ and provides an estimated sampling
distribution of the MI difference. The bootstrap
variation around the observed estimate could then be used to construct
an uncertainty interval for the population difference and assess whether
that interval includes zero.

An ordinary empirical bootstrap cannot sample an unobserved cell, because it
assigns that cell zero probability. It can therefore miss error arising from
unobserved cells. \citet{paninski2003} gives a broader warning: confidence
intervals based on resampling can be too narrow when information estimates
remain biased.

A simple permutation test instead combines the two samples and shuffles
their group labels. This gives an exact test when
the populations have the same complete distribution, \(P=Q\). Our hypothesis
requires only \(I(P)=I(Q)\): the tables can differ while their MI values are
equal. Equal MI alone does not guarantee that this label-permutation test
has the stated false-positive rate \citep{chung2013}.
Specialised permutation methods allow distinct
populations in some parameter comparisons \citep{janssen1997,chung2013};
their validity for equal MI would need to be established.
\section{Previous work and this thesis's contribution}

Existing work provides the leading bias and sampling variance of MI
\citep{miller1955,moddemeijer1989,brillinger2004,paninski2003}.
Hutcheson's entropy comparison assigns degrees of freedom from sample sizes
\citep{hutcheson1970}, while \citet{panwall2002} use the variability of a
regression variance estimate to choose degrees of freedom. Applying this
approach to MI requires calculating how the estimated MI variance changes
with the observed table, including changes to the cell probabilities,
row and column totals, and pointwise MI values.

This thesis derives how changes in the observed count table affect the
estimated MI variance and uses that result to calculate MI-specific degrees
of freedom for Expanded Welch. The resulting test retains Normal Wald's MI
difference and standard error but compares the statistic with a Student
\(t\) distribution rather than a standard normal distribution.

The experiment measures errors in the shared MI difference and standard
error alongside false-positive rates and power.
\citet{paninski2003} shows that finite-sample information estimates can
retain substantial bias after a leading correction. Such bias or an
inaccurate first-order variance approximation can undermine both tests,
even when Expanded Welch lowers rejection.

\chapter{Overview of the Two-Sample MI Test and Wald Baseline}
\label{chap:baselines}

Normal Wald and Expanded Welch share an estimated MI difference and standard
error. This chapter defines their statistic and the Normal Wald p-value.
\section{Problem setup and bias-corrected estimator}

Let
\begin{equation}
  N^P=(N^P_{ij}),
  \qquad
  N^Q=(N^Q_{ij})
\end{equation}
be independent \(r\times c\) count tables with totals \(n_P\) and \(n_Q\).
The rows and columns represent the same categorical variables \(X\) and
\(Y\) in both populations, with the same category definitions.
The empirical probabilities are
\begin{equation}
  \widehat p_{ij}=\frac{N^P_{ij}}{n_P},
  \qquad
  \widehat q_{ij}=\frac{N^Q_{ij}}{n_Q}.
\end{equation}
The large-sample argument uses the following assumptions.

\begin{assumption}[Aligned fixed alphabets]
The row and column categories are fixed in advance and aligned between the two
tables.
\end{assumption}

\begin{assumption}[Positive cell probabilities]
Every cell in the population table has a probability greater than zero. A
sample can still contain no observations in a cell, especially when that cell
is rare. Such samples remain in the study; we record how often cells have
zero observed counts to show how sparse the samples are.
\end{assumption}

\begin{assumption}[Positive MI]
Both populations have positive MI: \(I(P)>0\) and \(I(Q)>0\). With the positive
cell probabilities in Assumption~3, this is equivalent to requiring positive
first-order variances \(V(P)>0\) and \(V(Q)>0\). It excludes exact
independence, where the first-order approximation breaks down.
\end{assumption}

\begin{assumption}[Logarithm units]
All logarithms in this thesis are natural, so MI differences and standard
errors are reported in nats. Changing the logarithm base scales both by the
same positive constant and leaves the standardised statistic unchanged.
This is a choice of units, not a condition for the test to be valid.
\end{assumption}

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{Bias-corrected estimator.}
\section{Shared standard error and test statistic}

Section~\ref{sec:first-order-mi-background} showed that the first-order
sampling variance of \(\Ihat(P)\) is \(V(P)/n_P\), where \(V(P)\) is the
population variance of pointwise MI \citep{moddemeijer1989,brillinger2004}.
Subtracting the fixed leading bias term
in Equation~\eqref{eq:bias-corrected-difference} does not change this
variance.
\section[Normal Wald test and motivation for Expanded Welch]{Normal Wald test and motivation for\\Expanded Welch}

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{Why use a Student \(t\) distribution?}

Wald uses the standard normal distribution at every sample size, even
though its standard error is estimated from the observed tables. Expanded
Welch uses the variability of that variance estimate to choose a Student
\(t\) distribution instead.
Hutcheson's entropy test and ordinary Welch's test
set each variance component's degrees of freedom from its sample size:
\(n_i\) \citep{hutcheson1970} or \(n_i-1\) \citep{welch1947}. Neither assignment
measures how cell probabilities and margins make the estimated MI variance
change between samples.

To choose the degrees of freedom, we need the average value of each estimated
MI variance and how much that estimate varies across samples
\citep{satterthwaite1946}. For \(P\), to first order,
\begin{equation}
  \E\{\Vhat(P)\}\approx V(P).
\end{equation}
Chapter~\ref{chap:expanded} derives
\(\Var\{\Vhat(P)\}\) by tracking how the calculated MI variance changes
when one observation changes the joint table.

\chapter{Detailed Derivation of the Expanded Welch--Satterthwaite Test for MI}
\label{chap:expanded}

Expanded Welch keeps the estimated MI difference, standard error and test
statistic from Chapter~\ref{chap:baselines}, but changes the distribution used
to judge that statistic from the standard normal distribution to a Student
\(t\) distribution. To choose its degrees of freedom, this chapter calculates
how much the estimated MI variance changes between samples. The name
Expanded Welch refers to this expansion of the MI variance as the table
probabilities change.

\section[Choosing degrees of freedom for Expanded Welch]{Choosing degrees of
freedom for\\Expanded Welch}

The derivation has four steps. First, we relate the degrees of freedom to the
average and across-sample variation of \(\Vhat(P)\). Second, we calculate how \(V(P)\)
changes when a small amount of probability moves into one cell. Third, that
change tells us how variable \(\Vhat(P)\) is. Finally, we combine the
degrees of freedom from \(P\) and \(Q\) using Equation~\eqref{eq:ws-general}.

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{Moment matching for one MI variance estimate.}

\begin{samepage}
\section{How the MI variance changes with the table}

To find how much the estimated MI variance changes between samples, we first
ask how the population variance responds when a small amount of probability
is moved into one cell \citep{hampel1974,vanderVaart1998}. Fix a cell
\((x,y)\) and define the perturbed distribution
\begin{equation}
  P_\varepsilon
  =(1-\varepsilon)P+\varepsilon\delta_{(x,y)},
  \label{eq:contamination-path}
\end{equation}
where \(\delta_{(x,y)}\) places probability one on cell \((x,y)\). At
\(\varepsilon=0\), the distribution is \(P\). Increasing \(\varepsilon\)
moves a small amount of probability toward the selected cell while preserving
total probability one.
\par
\end{samepage}

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{Effect on pointwise MI and MI.}

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{Effect on the MI variance.}

Centred finite-difference checks on positive tables agreed with the MI
and variance derivatives to errors of order \(10^{-10}\). The experimental
supplement gives the checked tables and step size.
\section{Component degrees of freedom and final test}
\thesisminiheading{Population component degrees of freedom.}

\begin{assumption}[Regular variance sensitivity]
For the first-order Expanded Welch construction,
\(\tau^2(P)>0\) and \(\tau^2(Q)>0\).
\end{assumption}

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{Table-based component degrees of freedom.}

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{Combining the two samples' degrees of freedom.}

For a fixed finite \(T\), the Student \(t\) distribution gives a two-sided
p-value at least as large as the standard normal distribution used by Wald.
Under the implemented validity rules, every valid Expanded Welch result is
also Wald-valid, so every Expanded Welch rejection is also a Wald
rejection, including when invalid
outputs count as non-rejections in the reported rates. Expanded Welch cannot
raise rejection where Wald is already too conservative.
Appendix~\ref{sec:validity-rules} explains why a zero variance component
is excluded under the implemented validity rule.
\section{Worked example and implementation}

Consider the two observed \(3\times3\) tables
\begin{equation}
  N^P=
  \begin{pmatrix}
  35&10&5\\
  10&20&5\\
  5&5&10
  \end{pmatrix},
  \qquad
  N^Q=
  \begin{pmatrix}
  30&5&5\\
  5&30&5\\
  5&5&10
  \end{pmatrix}.
  \label{eq:worked-tables}
\end{equation}
Their totals are \(n_P=105\) and \(n_Q=100\). In \(N^P\), cell
\((1,1)\) has count 35, and its row and column each total 50. Its empirical
pointwise MI is therefore
\begin{equation*}
 \widehat\pmi_P(1,1)
 =\log\left\{\frac{35/105}{(50/105)(50/105)}\right\}
 =\log(1.47)\simeq0.38526.
\end{equation*}
This cell contributes \((35/105)(0.38526)\) to the plug-in MI estimate.
Summing the contributions from all nine cells gives
\(\Ihat(P)=0.13693\); the same calculation for \(N^Q\) gives
\(\Ihat(Q)=0.25848\) nats. Since \((3-1)(3-1)=4\), the corrected difference is
\begin{equation}
  \Deltahat
  =\left(0.13693-\frac{4}{2(105)}\right)
  -\left(0.25848-\frac{4}{2(100)}\right)
  =-0.12059.
\end{equation}

The variance calculation weights each squared deviation from the estimated
MI by its cell probability. Cell \((1,1)\), for example, contributes
\((35/105)(0.38526-0.13693)^2\simeq0.02056\) to \(\Vhat(P)\).
Summing over all cells gives \(\Vhat(P)=0.27189\) and
\(\Vhat(Q)=0.43371\). Hence
\begin{equation}
  \SEhat
  =\left(\frac{0.27189}{105}+\frac{0.43371}{100}\right)^{1/2}
  =0.08323,
  \qquad
  T=-1.44898.
\end{equation}
Normal Wald gives \(p=0.14734\).

For Expanded Welch, the same cell illustrates the sensitivity calculation.
The first row's pointwise-MI values are 0.38526, \(-0.51083\) and
\(-0.64436\), weighted by its counts 35, 10 and 5. Its conditional mean is
\begin{equation*}
 \frac{35(0.38526)+10(-0.51083)+5(-0.64436)}{50}
 \simeq0.10308.
\end{equation*}
Because this count table is symmetric, the first column has the same
conditional mean. Substituting these values into Equation~\eqref{eq:g-hat} gives
\begin{align*}
 \widehat g_P(1,1)
 &\simeq (0.38526-0.13693)^2-0.27189\\*
 &\quad+2\{0.38526-0.10308-0.10308+0.13693\}\\*
 &\simeq0.4218.
\end{align*}
The probability-weighted mean of the sensitivities is zero, so this cell
contributes \((35/105)(0.4218)^2\simeq0.0593\) to
\(\widehat\tau^2(P)\). Repeating the calculation for all cells in both
tables gives \(\widehat\tau^2(P)=0.93212\) and
\(\widehat\tau^2(Q)=0.82035\). Substitution into
Equation~\eqref{eq:nu-p-hat} gives component degrees of freedom
\begin{equation}
  \widehat\nu_P=16.65,
  \qquad
  \widehat\nu_Q=45.86.
\end{equation}
Combining them with Equation~\eqref{eq:expanded-df} gives
\(\widehat\nu_{\mathrm{expanded}}=59.03\) and \(p=0.15264\).
Neither method rejects at the 5\% level.

\section{Behaviour and limitations}
\label{sec:near-independence-mechanism}
\thesisminiheading{Near independence.}

Very close to independence, sampling noise itself creates apparent MI in
the empirical table. The resulting variance estimates need not be close to
their population values, so the estimated degrees of freedom need not tend
to zero with population MI at a fixed sample size. These local expansions
assume fixed table dimensions, positive cell probabilities and the
fixed-margin path. Appendix~\ref{sec:independence-boundary} retains the
quadratic sampling terms needed when population MI is very small.

Equations~\eqref{eq:mi-derivative} and \eqref{eq:g-final} are exact
derivatives for positive population tables and provide first-order
approximations to the sampling errors in MI and its estimated variance.
The scaled chi-squared model in Equation~\eqref{eq:scaled-chi-working} and
the Student \(t\) distribution for \(T\) are finite-sample approximations.
The MI difference and standard error come from the same tables. A sample
that changes the estimated difference can also change its standard error,
and Expanded Welch's larger cutoff does not account for how the estimated
MI difference and its standard error move together.
The experimental supplement gives the corresponding first-order
covariance calculation.
As sample sizes grow under regular conditions, the estimated
degrees of freedom increase and the Student \(t\) distribution approaches the
standard normal distribution used by Wald.
\par\nopagebreak[4]

Both tests need a finite corrected MI difference and a positive, finite
estimated standard error, while Expanded Welch also needs positive, finite component
and combined degrees of freedom. A failed requirement gives an invalid
calculation, not evidence for the null.
Appendix~\ref{sec:validity-rules} specifies the numerical criteria;
the experiment evaluates validity alongside calibration.

\chapter{Experimental Design}
\label{chap:design}

The simulations draw count tables from populations with known MI. This
allows us to measure errors in the estimated MI difference and its
standard error, and to count false positives when the population MI
values are equal. The evaluation addresses the two research questions in
Section~\ref{sec:research-questions}: whether the variance approximations
used by Expanded Welch are accurate, and how its false-positive rates
and power compare with those of Normal Wald. The design follows the simulation
framework of \citet{morris2019}, specifying the populations, quantities
being estimated, methods and performance measures.

One observation records an \((X,Y)\) outcome. One simulation repetition
draws a sample of observations from each population, producing two count
tables to which both tests are applied.
\section{Setup: Constructing joint distributions with known MI}

Before drawing samples, we construct population probability tables with
specified MI values. Equal MI values allow us to measure false-positive
rates, while different MI values allow us to measure power. For each table,
we first choose how frequently the categories occur, then change the
association between \(X\) and \(Y\) while keeping those frequencies fixed.

The main simulations use square tables. Both variables have \(k\)
categories, labelled \(1,\ldots,k\), so the joint distribution has
\(k\times k\) cells. Let \(a=(a_1,\ldots,a_k)\) specify the category
frequencies: \(a_i\) is the probability of category \(i\), with
\(a_i>0\) and \(\sum_i a_i=1\). Within one population, we use this same
vector for both variables. Thus \(a\) specifies the row margins for
\(X\) and the column margins for \(Y\).

To obtain independent variables, we could draw \(X\) using \(a\), then
draw \(Y\) independently using \(a\). Cell \((i,j)\) would have
probability \(a_i a_j\), and MI would be zero. We introduce dependence
by allowing \(Y\) to copy the category drawn for \(X\) on some
observations. Let \(\lambda\) be the probability of copying. For each
observation, first draw \(X\) using \(a\), then choose between two ways
of generating \(Y\), independently of the value of \(X\):
\begin{itemize}
 \item With probability \(\lambda\), set \(Y=X\).
 \item With probability \(1-\lambda\), draw \(Y\) independently using \(a\).
\end{itemize}
An independent draw can still match \(X\) by chance, whereas copying
guarantees a match. Increasing \(\lambda\) therefore makes matching
categories occur more often.

Both choices preserve the category frequencies of \(Y\). When \(Y\)
copies \(X\), its categories have probabilities \(a\) because those are
the probabilities used to draw \(X\). An independent draw of \(Y\)
also uses \(a\). Consequently, changing how often we copy changes which
categories occur together, while the row and column margins remain fixed.
Sample row and column proportions fluctuate around these population
probabilities.

To calculate a cell probability, add the contributions from the two
choices. The independent choice is made with probability \(1-\lambda\)
and produces \(X=i,Y=j\) with probability \(a_i a_j\), contributing
\((1-\lambda)a_i a_j\). The copying choice contributes only to diagonal
cells, where the categories match. Reaching cell \((i,i)\) requires both
copying and \(X=i\), so its contribution is \(\lambda a_i\).
Write \(\mathbf{1}_{\{i=j\}}\) for an indicator that equals one when
\(i=j\) and zero otherwise. Adding the two contributions gives
\begin{equation}
 p_{ij}(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)a_i a_j
                  +\lambda a_i\mathbf{1}_{\{i=j\}},
 \qquad 0\leq\lambda<1,
 \label{eq:copying-construction}
\end{equation}
where the restriction \(\lambda<1\) keeps the independent choice possible
and therefore gives every cell positive probability. This copying
construction is a special case of the mixture model described by
\citet{bocci2010}.

At \(\lambda=0\), MI is zero. Increasing \(\lambda\) increases MI,
although the copying probability needed to reach a particular MI depends
on the category frequencies \(a\). To construct a table with the desired
MI, we hold \(a\) fixed and search numerically for \(\lambda\),
calculating MI from the population table at each candidate value.
Appendix~\ref{app:construction} gives the available MI range, the numerical
search and the fixed-margin calculation.

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{Constructing a \(2\times2\) joint distribution with positive MI.}

For population \(P\), take \(a=(0.7,0.3)\). Each variable therefore has
probability 0.7 of taking category 1 and probability 0.3 of taking
category 2. Choose a target MI of 0.02 nats. The numerical search gives
a copying probability of approximately 0.20347.

Cell \((1,1)\) requires \(X=1\), which has probability 0.7. Given
\(X=1\), copying always gives \(Y=1\), while an independent draw gives
\(Y=1\) with probability 0.7. Cell \((1,2)\) also requires \(X=1\),
but copying cannot give \(Y=2\). It therefore requires the independent
choice followed by a draw of category 2, which has probability 0.3.
Multiplying these conditional probabilities by the probability of
\(X=1\) gives
\begin{align*}
 p_{11}&\simeq0.7\{0.20347+(1-0.20347)(0.7)\}=0.53273,\\
 p_{12}&\simeq0.7(1-0.20347)(0.3)=0.16727.
\end{align*}
Both off-diagonal cells have probability \((1-\lambda)(0.7)(0.3)\), so
\(p_{21}=p_{12}\). The second row totals 0.3, giving
\(p_{22}\simeq0.3-0.16727=0.13273\).

For population \(Q\), use \(a=(0.8,0.2)\) and a target MI of 0.03 nats.
Its numerical search gives
a copying probability of approximately 0.26091. The resulting tables are
\begin{equation}
 P\simeq\begin{pmatrix}0.53273&0.16727\\0.16727&0.13273\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 Q\simeq\begin{pmatrix}0.68175&0.11825\\0.11825&0.08175\end{pmatrix}.
 \label{eq:design-example-pair}
\end{equation}
These tables have \(I(P)=0.02\) and \(I(Q)=0.03\) nats, so the true
signed difference is \(\Delta=I(P)-I(Q)=-0.01\) nats. To construct an
equal-MI comparison, we instead choose the
same target MI for both populations and search for each copying
probability separately.

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{Table sizes and margin regimes.}

The experiment repeats this construction for square tables of sizes
\(2\times2,4\times4,8\times8\) and \(16\times16\), containing
4, 16, 64 and 256 cells. Each doubling of the number of categories
multiplies the number of cells by four. At a fixed sample size,
observations must then be distributed over more possible cells.

Table~\ref{tab:margin-profiles} specifies the three regimes. Same skew
uses the same uneven frequencies in both populations; different skew
uses a first-category probability of 0.7 in \(P\) and 0.8 in \(Q\).
Thus the row and column margins agree within each population, while the
margins can differ between populations.

Under equal MI, the uniform and same-skew regimes give identical joint
probability tables, \(P=Q\): both populations have the same margins and
the same copying probability. The different-skew regime instead gives
different tables with equal MI because the category frequencies differ.
Comparing the regimes therefore measures false positives under both
identical tables and distinct tables with equal MI.
\section{RQ1: Checking the variance approximations}

Expanded Welch chooses its component degrees of freedom from
\(\E\{\Vhat(P)\}\) and \(\Var\{\Vhat(P)\}\), and likewise for \(Q\).
To check these quantities, we hold the
population table \(P\) and sample size \(n_P\) fixed, then draw repeated
count tables. Each draw gives a new \(\Vhat(P)\), which estimates the
pointwise-MI variance \(V(P)\). Dividing by \(n_P\) gives that
population's estimated contribution to the variance of the MI difference.
The average of the \(\Vhat(P)\) values estimates \(\E\{\Vhat(P)\}\);
their variation across draws estimates \(\Var\{\Vhat(P)\}\).

We next examine how the moment approximations affect the degrees of
freedom. Using the actual sampling moments gives the component target
\begin{equation}
 \nu_{P,\mathrm{mom}}
 =\frac{2\{\E\Vhat(P)\}^{2}}{\Var\{\Vhat(P)\}}.
 \label{eq:design-moment-target}
\end{equation}
The repeated samples estimate the mean and variance in this expression.
We compare both the population first-order degrees of freedom and the
average estimated component degrees of freedom with this target. For the
latter, the ratio
\(\operatorname{mean}(\widehat\nu_P)/\nu_{P,\mathrm{mom}}\) equals one
when the average estimate matches the target; a ratio below one means
that the estimated degrees of freedom are lower on average. Medians and
percentile ranges describe their sampling spread. When a summary uses only
positive finite degrees of freedom, we report the included fraction. The
same checks are made for \(Q\).
Appendix~\ref{sec:moment-target-details} gives the definitions and algebra.

\section{RQ2.1: False-positive rates under equal MI}

To measure false positives, we set the two population MI values equal and
draw a count table from each population in every repetition. Every
rejection is then a false positive. Normal Wald and Expanded Welch use the same bias-corrected MI
difference and estimated standard error from
Chapter~\ref{chap:baselines}. Their cutoffs differ: Normal Wald uses the
standard normal distribution, while Expanded Welch uses a Student \(t\)
distribution with MI-specific degrees of freedom estimated from the two
sampled count tables.

Both tests use a two-sided 5\% nominal test. The broad null comparison
uses the first grid in Table~\ref{tab:design-primary-grids}: common MI
0.02 nats, four table sizes, three margin regimes and ten sample sizes,
giving 120 settings. At each setting, a false-positive rate above 5\%
means excessive rejection; a rate below 5\% means conservative rejection.
We also report the fraction of valid results, because an unusable
calculation contributes no rejection.

To check whether rejection behaviour depends on the association
construction, a supporting comparison replaces copying by a probability
transfer within four cells while preserving the margins and target MI.
The experimental supplement reports the full construction results.
\section{RQ2.2: Nominal and calibrated power}

Power is the probability of rejecting equal MI when the population MI
values differ. We first compare power using the nominal 5\% cutoffs.
A test that rejects less often under equal MI can also reject less often
under alternatives, so we then compare power after adjusting the cutoffs
to match rejection at a specified equal-MI population.

The focused comparison uses settings A--C in
Table~\ref{tab:redesign-focus-settings}. Earlier simulations identified
A and B as settings where Expanded Welch brought false-positive rates
closer to 5\%; their power is evaluated on new independent samples.
Setting C provides a larger-sample comparison.

To choose the MI differences for a power curve, we first measure the
sampling variation under equal MI. An independent null simulation
estimates the standard deviation (SD) of the corrected MI difference;
denote this fitted value by \(\sigma_0\). Measuring differences in units
of \(\sigma_0\) makes the three curves comparable relative to their null
sampling variation.

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{Power after matching null rejection.}

Empirical calibration chooses a p-value threshold separately for each
test. For each full power curve, the
procedure is:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item Use the independent fitting samples with \(I(P)=I(Q)=0.02\) nats,
 retaining the curve's margins, table size and sample sizes.
 \item Choose each rule's threshold to give at most 5\% rejection in
 that fitting batch, and hold it fixed across the curve.
 \item Apply the thresholds to separate equal-MI evaluation samples and
 to the alternative samples, measuring the achieved false-positive rates
 and power.
\end{enumerate}
Normal Wald orders samples by \(|T|\): larger \(|T|\) always gives a
smaller p-value.
Expanded Welch can order samples differently because its degrees of
freedom change with the sampled count tables.

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{Changing the calibration population.}

Equal MI can occur at different common MI values. To examine how that
choice affects the power comparison, we repeat calibration at \(h=2\)
and \(h=4\) for A--C using the two null populations in
Table~\ref{tab:design-calibration-populations}.

The lower null sets both
MI values to the alternative's smaller value; the upper null sets both
to its larger value. Both retain the alternative's margins and sample sizes.

Independent upper-null batches fit and validate the new cutoffs. We apply
both calibrations to the same alternative simulation outputs, so any
change in measured power comes from the cutoffs rather than a change of alternative samples.
Each calibration is also evaluated at both nulls. Matching rejection at
one null population does not ensure the same false-positive rate elsewhere
under equal MI. Appendix~\ref{sec:calibration-sensitivity-design} gives
the construction and uncertainty calculation.

The experimental supplement reports broader MI differences from 0 to
0.2 nats at \(n=1{,}000\) and 10,000, and a separate sample-allocation
analysis. The experimental supplement specifies those additional settings.

the companion uniform and same-skew plots.

\subsection{How moment errors affect degrees of freedom}

Equation~\eqref{eq:design-moment-target} defines
\(\nu_{P,\mathrm{mom}}\) from \(\E\{\Vhat(P)\}\) and
\(\Var\{\Vhat(P)\}\). We compare this target with \(\nu_P\),
calculated using the population first-order approximations, and
\(\widehat\nu_P\), estimated from each sampled table. Their differences show how the moment approximations and the
substitution of sample proportions affect the degrees of freedom.

For the same different-skew populations,
Figure~\ref{fig:redesign-component-df} uses the moment target,
estimated from the simulations, as the common denominator. The top row shows
\(\nu_P/\nu_{P,\mathrm{mom}}\); the bottom row shows
\(\E(\widehat\nu_P)/\nu_{P,\mathrm{mom}}\), and likewise for \(Q\).
Both rows use the same vertical scale. Ratios below one mean too few
degrees of freedom; ratios above one mean too many. Bottom-row curves
require all component estimates to be positive and finite. Shading in
the top row gives approximate 95\% Monte Carlo intervals.

Underestimating \(\E\{\Vhat(P)\}\) lowers \(\nu_P\) relative to
\(\nu_{P,\mathrm{mom}}\). For different-skew
\(4\times4\) populations at \(n=1{,}000\) and MI 0.02, the
predicted / observed sampling-variance ratios are 0.970 for \(P\) and
0.967 for \(Q\).
The observed means are \(1.190V(P)\) and \(1.174V(Q)\). The first-order
calculation substitutes \(V(P)\) for the larger sampling mean
\(\E\Vhat(P)\), and likewise for \(Q\). Because the moment-matching
formula squares the mean, this substitution lowers the degrees of freedom
even though the sampling-variance prediction is close. The resulting
first-order values, 15.30 and 13.61, fall below the moment targets,
21.03 and 18.14. Table~\ref{tab:variance-stability} gives the component
values; Appendix~\ref{sec:moment-target-details} gives the algebra.

In the table, ``Mean ratio'' is the observed mean of \(\Vhat(P)\)
divided by \(V(P)\), or the corresponding ratio for \(Q\).
``Var. ratio (pop.)'' and ``Var. ratio (sample)'' divide
\(\tau^2(P)/n_P\) and the average \(\widehat\tau^2(P)/n_P\),
respectively, by the same observed \(\Var\{\Vhat(P)\}\), with
corresponding calculations for \(Q\). ``Mean df'' averages
\(\widehat\nu_P\) or \(\widehat\nu_Q\) over positive finite estimates;
all 100,000 are included in each shown row. ``Moment df'' gives
\(\nu_{P,\mathrm{mom}}\) or \(\nu_{Q,\mathrm{mom}}\), while ``FO df''
gives \(\nu_P\) or \(\nu_Q\).

Mean estimated component degrees of freedom can also fall below their
moment targets (Table~\ref{tab:redesign-component-spread}). At A (uniform
\(4\times4\), \(n_P=n_Q=20\)), the \(P\) target is 14.81 against
an average estimate of 6.52, giving an estimate / target ratio of 0.44.
For the \(16\times16\), \(n=1{,}000\) same- and different-skew cases,
these ratios range from 0.55 to 0.60. All 100,000 component estimates
are included in these comparisons. At C (different-skew \(4\times4\),
\(n_P=n_Q=10{,}000\)), the ratios are about 0.99.
The bottom row of Figure~\ref{fig:redesign-component-df} shows the discrepancy when
population probabilities in the first-order formula are replaced by
sample proportions. The moment target itself does not guarantee an
exact Student \(t\) distribution for the test statistic.

\FloatBarrier
\subsection{Behaviour near independence}

As MI approaches zero, \(V(P)\) and \(V(Q)\) become small. Terms
quadratic in the sampling error can then contribute substantially to
\(\Vhat(P)\) and \(\Vhat(Q)\), so the first-order predictions need
not remain accurate. The near-independence calculation in
Appendix~\ref{sec:independence-boundary} retains these quadratic terms
to approximate the component moments and estimated degrees of freedom.

Figure~\ref{fig:redesign-a4} shows \(4\times4\) different-skew
populations at \(n=1{,}000\). The first two rows compare the observed
moments of \(\Vhat\) with their near-independence predictions. The
bottom row compares the mean estimated degrees of freedom, its
near-independence prediction, the sampling-moment target and the
population first-order value.

At common MI 0.0001, the near-independence calculation predicts
\(n\E\{\Vhat(P)\}=9.2\) for each population; the observed value for
\(P\) is 9.158. The mean estimated component degrees of freedom for
\(P\) are 4.86, close to the prediction 4.6, while the sampling-moment
target is about nine. Thus the near-independence calculation describes
the mean estimated degrees of freedom accurately even though that mean
remains below the moment target. The experimental supplement retains
the median, percentile range and near-independence prediction of the
moment target in the full diagnostic plots.

Near independence, Table~\ref{tab:variance-stability} shows opposite
errors for the first-order population and sample-based predictions. At the smallest MI target in
Figure~\ref{fig:redesign-a4}, \(\tau^2(P)/n_P\) and \(\tau^2(Q)/n_Q\)
are only about 5\% of the observed sampling variances. The mean
sample-based predictions are instead 1.97 times the observed variance
for \(P\) and 2.14 times for \(Q\), indicating overprediction.
The quadratic sampling contribution remains substantial, while the
population first-order degrees of freedom are below 0.1.

At MI 0.02, \(\tau^2(P)/n_P\) and \(\tau^2(Q)/n_Q\) are much more
accurate. The sample-based predictions still overestimate variation:
their predicted / observed ratios are 1.080 for \(P\) and 1.072 for \(Q\). The remaining mean error still lowers
the first-order degrees of freedom relative to the moment target.
Appendix~\ref{sec:component-diagnostics} reports the mean error across
MI and margins.
\section{RQ2.1: False-positive rates under equal MI}

We now set \(I(P)=I(Q)\), so every rejection is a false positive.
Both tests use \(T=\Deltahat/\SEhat\), but Expanded Welch uses a
cutoff from the Student \(t\) distribution in place of Wald's standard
normal cutoff. This larger cutoff reduces rejection. Whether that
reduction improves accuracy depends on whether Wald's rate exceeds or
falls below the nominal 5\% level.

\subsection{Overall false-positive patterns}
\label{sec:null-rejection-patterns}

Expanded Welch improves false-positive rates in selected settings where
Normal Wald rejects too often. In others, it further lowers already
conservative rates. Table~\ref{tab:redesign-null-grid} summarises the
120 settings at common MI 0.02 nats.

We classify Expanded Welch as improving a setting when its false-positive
rate is closer to 5\% than Wald's by more than
\RedesignGridTolerance{} percentage points. It worsens a setting when its
rate is farther from 5\% by more than \RedesignGridTolerance{} percentage
points. Differences within this tolerance are grouped separately. All
\RedesignToward{} improvements occur with Wald above 5\%;
\RedesignAwayBelow{} of the \RedesignAway{} deteriorations occur with
Wald below 5\%.

Reported rejection rates divide valid rejections by all simulation
repetitions, counting invalid outputs as non-rejections. Brackets around
rates and shading in rejection plots give pointwise 95\% intervals for
uncertainty from the finite simulation batch.

Figures~\ref{fig:redesign-null-uniform} and
\ref{fig:redesign-null-different} show uniform and different-skew margins.
The lower panels give the fraction of valid outputs for each test.
Validity is lowest in the smallest samples: across the 120 settings,
the minimum valid fractions are 0.958 for Normal Wald and 0.631 for
Expanded Welch. The supplement reports conditional rates and
included counts separately.

To explain these rejection rates, we examine the two shared estimates.
Difference bias measures how far the average \(\Deltahat\) lies from
\(\Delta\). The variance ratio for \(\Deltahat\) divides the average
\(\SEhat^2\) by the observed \(\Var(\Deltahat)\). A ratio below one
means that the squared standard error underestimates sampling variance;
a ratio above one means that it overestimates sampling variance.
These diagnostics distinguish a shifted estimated difference from an
inaccurate standard error. Table~\ref{tab:redesign-shared-estimates}
compares the focus settings and the sparse \(16\times16\) cases at
\(n=1{,}000\). The full diagnostics, including the larger-sample
\(16\times16\) cases, remain in Table~\ref{tab:redesign-case-diagnostics}.

Expanded Welch brings rejection close to 5\% at A. At B it also
reduces rejection, although the rate remains above 5\%.
Table~\ref{tab:redesign-case-rates} compares these settings with the
larger-sample and sparse-table cases. Both tests are valid in all
100,000 repetitions at each of these seven settings.

At A, difference bias is negligible, but \(\SEhat\) understates the
variation of \(\Deltahat\). At B, \(\Deltahat\) is biased upwards
and the average \(\SEhat^2\) exceeds the observed
\(\Var(\Deltahat)\). Expanded Welch lowers false positives in both
cases despite these different estimation errors. At C, bias is negligible
and the variance ratio is close to one. Table~\ref{tab:redesign-case-diagnostics}
gives the full diagnostics and degrees-of-freedom comparisons.

Both tests also over-reject at stronger common MI. Table~\ref{tab:redesign-stronger-null}
retains A's and B's margins, table sizes and sample sizes while increasing
the common MI. Rates and their pointwise 95\% intervals are percentages
of all 100,000 repetitions.

Changing the degrees of freedom does not resolve the sparse-table
failure. At \(16\times16\), different skew and \(n=1{,}000\), the
difference bias is about 0.030 nats, or 2.06 observed SDs. Both tests
reject far too often; changing the rejection cutoff leaves the bias
unchanged.
Under the equal-MI null, the estimated difference is centred at
\begin{equation}
 \E(\Deltahat)\approx 0+0.02985=0.02985\text{ nats}.
 \label{eq:redesign-null-bias-shift}
\end{equation}
This shift is large relative to the observed SD of approximately 0.01450
nats. It moves most rejections into the positive tail even though the
population difference is zero.

Under equal MI, the same-skew populations have identical tables. With
equal sample sizes, their expected MI estimation biases therefore cancel
in the difference. The average \(\SEhat^2\) exceeds the observed
\(\Var(\Deltahat)\), and both rejection rates are far below 5\%.
The matched populations distinguish rejection driven by a large
difference bias from conservative behaviour when that bias cancels.
At \(n=10{,}000\), both skew regimes have much smaller estimation errors
and rates closer to 5\%.

The sparse-table failure also occurs under the four-cell construction.
At \(16\times16\), common MI 0.02 nats and
\(n_P=n_Q=1{,}000\), replacing copying by a probability transfer
within four cells preserves each population's margins and MI.
Under different-skew margins, the estimated difference remains
substantially biased and both false-positive rates are near 30\%.
The experimental supplement reports the full construction comparison.
\section{RQ2.2: Nominal and calibrated power}

The power comparison uses A (uniform \(4\times4\), \(n_P=n_Q=20\)),
B (different-skew \(8\times8\), \(n_P=n_Q=100\)) and
C (different-skew \(4\times4\), \(n_P=n_Q=10{,}000\)). For each
setting, \(\sigma_0\) is the independently fitted SD of \(\Deltahat\)
under \(I(P)=I(Q)=0.02\) nats. We hold \(I(P)=0.02\) and increase
\(I(Q)\), so \(\Delta=I(P)-I(Q)\) is negative under the alternatives.
The horizontal axis is \(-\Delta/\sigma_0\): moving right increases
the MI advantage of \(Q\) in fitted null SD units.
Nominal power uses each test's usual 5\% cutoff; calibrated power uses
cutoffs fitted to target 5\% rejection at a specified equal-MI population.
\subsection{Nominal power}

Expanded Welch has lower nominal power than Normal Wald at the selected
small-sample settings A and B (Table~\ref{tab:redesign-focus-settings}).
At A, two null SDs correspond to about 0.310 nats: Expanded Welch rejects
35.9\% of repetitions, compared with 41.0\% for Wald.
Figure~\ref{fig:redesign-power} shows all three focus settings with MI
differences measured in fitted null standard deviations. The nominal
comparison includes their different null rejection rates at zero.
Appendix~\ref{sec:calibration-sensitivity-results} gives numerical rates
and differences between methods evaluated on the same simulated data.

As the population MI values move farther apart at B, rejection initially
falls before rising. Expanded Welch's rate falls from 5.52\% under the null to
1.99\% at one null SD, before rising to 33.1\% at four SDs. As
\(I(Q)\) increases, the true signed difference becomes negative,
initially offsetting the positive estimation bias observed under the
null. The estimated difference moves towards zero, reducing \(|T|\)
and rejection before the curve rises. This distortion of the shared
statistic remains when the rejection cutoff is increased.
Appendix~\ref{app:additional-results} reports the estimated directions
among rejections in the sparse-table comparisons.

At C, nominal power differences are small. At two null SDs, or about
0.00635 nats, Wald gives 45.2\% and Expanded Welch gives 44.9\%.
Expanded Welch's loss relative to Wald is 0.30 percentage points,
with a 95\% interval of 0.27--0.34. Table~\ref{tab:redesign-power-contrasts}
reports comparisons at two null SDs for all three focus settings.
Each interval uses both methods' decisions from the same simulation
repetitions to estimate their power difference. These are paired
comparisons: the pairing is between methods applied to the same data.
The calibrated comparison then assesses power after matching null rejection.

\FloatBarrier
\subsection{Power after matching false-positive rates}

At settings A and B, Expanded Welch's lower nominal power accompanies a
lower false-positive rate than Normal Wald's. We now ask whether its
power remains lower after adjusting both tests to have approximately the
same false-positive rate.

Empirical calibration fits a separate p-value threshold for each test
using independent equal-MI simulations to target 5\% rejection. These
replace the usual threshold of 0.05. We hold them fixed, check their
false-positive rates on
independent equal-MI samples, and apply them to the same alternative
samples used in the nominal comparison. The MI difference \(\Deltahat\),
standard error \(\SEhat\) and calculated p-values remain unchanged.

We first fit the thresholds at \(I(P)=I(Q)=0.02\) nats. On independent
null evaluation samples, both tests reject between 4.93\% and 4.99\%
across A--C, so their false-positive rates are closely matched there.
Figure~\ref{fig:redesign-calibrated-power} shows rejection under these
thresholds: at zero on the horizontal axis it measures false positives;
to the right, it measures power against increasing MI differences.

\begin{samepage}
At A and two null SDs, Normal Wald has calibrated power of 32.57\%,
compared with 36.15\% for Expanded Welch: a gain of 3.58 percentage
points. Thus the nominal power ordering reverses at this alternative
after matching false-positive rates at common MI 0.02.
\par
\end{samepage}

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{Does the calibration population change the comparison?}

The first comparison matches false-positive rates at common MI 0.02.
We next ask whether Expanded Welch's power advantage persists when the
thresholds are fitted at a different common MI.

For an alternative with \(I(P)=0.02\) and \(I(Q)>0.02\), we compare:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item \textbf{Lower-null calibration:} fit both tests at
  \(I(P)=I(Q)=0.02\), the alternative's smaller MI.
  \item \textbf{Upper-null calibration:} fit both tests with their
  population MI values equal to the alternative's larger \(I(Q)\).
\end{itemize}
Both calibration populations retain the alternative's margins and sample
sizes. Applying both sets of thresholds to the same alternative samples
ensures that only the thresholds change the power comparison.

Table~\ref{tab:redesign-calibration-sensitivity} reports Expanded Welch
power minus Normal Wald power at two and four null SDs. Gains are in
percentage points: positive values favour Expanded Welch and negative
values favour Wald. The upper-MI column gives the common MI used for
upper-null fitting. Brackets give 95\% bootstrap intervals accounting
for the shared evaluation data and uncertainty from fitting thresholds.

Changing the fitting population reverses the gain in two comparisons.
At A and two null SDs, the 3.58-point gain becomes a 0.76-point loss.
At B and four SDs, a 3.92-point gain becomes a 0.39-point loss.
Under upper-null calibration, A at four SDs retains a small positive
estimate whose interval includes zero, while B at two SDs retains a much
smaller gain. At C, both calibrations give differences well within the
one-percentage-point tolerance.

The calibrated gains therefore depend on where we match false-positive
rates. Appendix~\ref{sec:calibration-sensitivity-results} reports the
rates from applying each calibration to both null populations and the
full power tables. Matching at one population does not ensure matching
elsewhere. These two checks also do not establish that either test keeps
its false-positive rate at or below 5\% for every equal-MI population.

\section{Application to online shopping data}
\label{sec:shoppers-application}

The Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention dataset records website sessions
and whether each session ends in a purchase \citep{sakar2018}. We use it
to address two application questions:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\arabic*.},leftmargin=*,nosep]
  \item \textbf{Month:} Does month provide the same amount of information
  about purchasing among new and returning visitors?
  \item \textbf{Weekend:} Does weekend status provide the same amount of
  information about purchasing among new and returning visitors?
\end{enumerate}

The dataset contains 12,330 sessions, with each session belonging to a
different user according to the source documentation \citep{sakar2018}.
The analysis retains all 1,694 sessions labelled \texttt{New\_Visitor}
and 10,551 labelled \texttt{Returning\_Visitor}, excluding the 85
\texttt{Other} sessions. The outcome is the original Boolean
\texttt{Revenue} variable: true indicates a purchase and false indicates
no purchase. The tests treat the two disjoint visitor groups as independent
samples and the sessions within each group as independent observations.

For each question, \(X\) is the session attribute and \(Y\) is the
purchase outcome. The two populations are defined by visitor type:

\label{tab:shoppers-questions}

\toprule
 & Month question & Weekend question\\
\midrule
\(X\) & Month of the session & Weekday or weekend\\
\(Y\) & \multicolumn{2}{l}{Purchase outcome: no purchase or purchase}\\
\(P\) & \multicolumn{2}{l}{Joint distribution of \((X,Y)\) among new visitors}\\

For month, each group forms a \(10\times2\) count table. The rows are
the ten recorded months: February, March, May, June, July, August,
September, October, November and December. The columns are no purchase
and purchase. Both groups use these categories, with no smoothing or
removal of zero cells. All ten months occur in both groups, although the
new-visitor February row contains only one session and no purchase.
Replacing month with the Boolean \texttt{Weekend} variable gives a
\(2\times2\) table for each group, with weekday and weekend rows;
all four cells are observed.

The leading MI bias correction subtracts
\((10-1)(2-1)/(2n)=9/(2n)\) from each month plug-in estimate
\citep{miller1955,moddemeijer1989}, and \(1/(2n)\) from each weekend
estimate, where \(n\) is the relevant group size. The corrected
difference \(\Deltahat\) is new-visitor MI minus returning-visitor MI.
Table~\ref{tab:shoppers-application} gives these differences alongside
their shared standard errors, \(\SEhat\), and the resulting
\(T=\Deltahat/\SEhat\). MI estimates, differences and standard errors
are in nats.

Both tests reject equal month--purchase MI. Expanded Welch's larger
p-value reflects the heavier tails of the Student \(t\) distribution
with 26.79 degrees of freedom.

For weekend, both corrected MI estimates are approximately 0.0007 nats.
Their difference is only about 0.056 standard errors from zero, so both
