\chapter{Conclusions}
\label{chap:conclusion}
\section{Contributions and main findings}

This thesis derives an Expanded Welch--Satterthwaite test for comparing
categorical MI across independent populations. Its mathematical
contribution is the observation-level sensitivity of the estimated MI
variance, accounting for changes in cell probabilities, margins and
pointwise MI. The variance of this sensitivity gives a first-order
sampling-variance approximation, which is used with moment matching to
choose MI-specific degrees of freedom for a Student \(t\) distribution.
\subsection{RQ1: Accuracy of variance approximations}

The mean and sampling variance of \(\Vhat(P)\) need separate checks.
The predicted sampling variance can be close to its observed value while
the mean estimate remains above \(V(P)\). In the moment target in
Equation~\eqref{eq:design-moment-target}, the mean is squared in the
numerator. Replacing the inflated sampling mean by the smaller population
value therefore lowers the population first-order degrees of freedom,
even when the sampling-variance approximation is accurate. The mean
estimated component degrees of freedom can fall further below the moment
target when population probabilities are replaced by sample proportions.
The size of these discrepancies depends on the population and sample size.

Near independence, the first-order prediction \(\tau^2(P)/n_P\) for
\(\Var\{\Vhat(P)\}\) is small and quadratic sampling terms remain
substantial. The calculation in
Appendix~\ref{sec:independence-boundary} explains the observed scale of
the estimated component degrees of freedom. These results
explain why the first-order approximation becomes inadequate near
independence and why substituting sample probabilities requires its own
evaluation, even when the population approximation is accurate.
\subsection{RQ2.1: False-positive rates under equal MI}

Expanded Welch brings false-positive rates closer to 5\% in the selected
small-sample settings A and B, both at common MI 0.02 nats
(Table~\ref{tab:redesign-focus-settings}). Both tests return valid results
in every repetition at these settings, so the lower rejection rates
reflect the larger cutoff from the Student \(t\) distribution. Across the
broad grid, Expanded Welch also lowers rates that are already below 5\%.
Its larger cutoff helps when it corrects excessive rejection and increases
conservatism when rejection is already too infrequent.

A false-positive rate near 5\% does not establish that the estimated
degrees of freedom accurately match the denominator's sampling moments.
At A, the standard error understates the observed sampling variation of
the MI difference, while the low estimated degrees of freedom increase
the rejection cutoff. These errors can compensate in the false-positive
rate. At B, the average squared standard error exceeds the observed
variance of the MI difference and the difference is biased, so the same
explanation does not apply unchanged.

The sparse same-skew null illustrates how error in the standard error can
remain when the expected difference bias cancels. Identical population
tables at equal sample sizes have the same expected MI estimation bias.
However, the average \(\SEhat^2\) is almost twice the observed
\(\Var(\Deltahat)\) in the sparse copying case, and both tests are
conservative. Unequal sample sizes can also leave unequal residual biases
in otherwise identical populations. Reliable testing therefore requires
accurate estimation of both the MI difference and its uncertainty.
\subsection{RQ2.2: Nominal and calibrated power}

Expanded Welch has lower nominal power than Normal Wald at the selected
small-sample settings A and B. Because the two tests also have different
false-positive rates, the calibrated comparison adjusts their cutoffs to
match rejection at a specified equal-MI population before comparing power.
At common MI 0.02 nats, Expanded Welch gains power over Wald at A and B.
Moving calibration to the upper equal-MI population while holding the
alternative fixed reverses the gain at A and two null SDs, and at B and
four null SDs (Table~\ref{tab:redesign-calibration-sensitivity}). At C,
nominal power differences are small and calibrated differences remain
practically small under both calibrations.

The calibrated power advantage depends on the population used to fit the
cutoff. Matching false-positive rates at the lower common MI does not
ensure that the two tests have the same false-positive rate at the upper
common MI. Expanded Welch's sample-dependent degrees of freedom can change
the ordering of datasets by their p-values, but the observed gains do not
establish a stable power advantage across the equal-MI null.

Changing the cutoff also leaves errors in the estimated MI difference
unchanged. At B, positive estimation bias initially offsets the negative
true difference as \(I(Q)\) increases. The estimated difference moves
towards zero, so rejection initially falls even though the population MI
values move farther apart. This distortion remains after calibration.

The sparse \(16\times16\) different-skew comparison shows a more severe
failure. Its positive difference bias exceeds the true negative difference
at the 0.01-nat alternative, so almost every rejection gives the wrong
estimated ordering. Equation~\eqref{eq:redesign-alternative-bias-shift}
explains the sign reversal. The four-cell construction also reproduces
the sparse-table failure. A larger rejection cutoff cannot correct that bias.
\section{Limitations}

The derivation assumes independent categorical observations, fixed
categories, positive population cell probabilities and positive
first-order MI variance. Paired samples would require a covariance term
in the difference variance. Growing alphabets and continuous MI estimators
have different approximation errors. Exact independence requires the
second-order argument in Appendix~\ref{sec:independence-boundary}.

The findings concern the tested populations, association constructions and
alternative paths. The power settings were selected using earlier
false-positive results and evaluated on independent samples. Each curve
keeps \(I(P)=0.02\) and increases \(I(Q)\) along the copying family.
Both tested constructions use equal row and column margins within each
table and align association locations between populations. Other directions
of MI change, unequal row and column margins within a table and other
locations of dependence remain untested. The results therefore support
further investigation of Expanded Welch rather than its use as a general
replacement for Normal Wald.

Empirical calibration uses known simulation populations. The two calibration
checks do not bound rejection across the entire equal-MI null or supply
a calibration procedure for arbitrary observed tables. The pointwise
confidence intervals quantify simulation uncertainty for the specified
populations; the calibrated power intervals also include uncertainty from
fitting the cutoffs.

The online-shopping application illustrates how to report the estimated
MI difference and its direction, standard error, p-value and Expanded Welch
degrees of freedom. Its unknown population MI values prevent a direct
check of false-positive rates. The application therefore demonstrates
interpretation of the test outputs, while the simulation evidence
establishes their behaviour under known populations.
\section{Future work}

A first extension is to derive the second-order mean contribution to the
variance estimator and evaluate a corresponding degrees-of-freedom
correction. The observed variation across MI and margins indicates that
the correction should depend on the population table. A fixed coefficient
based only on table size would leave errors in some settings. Any
estimated correction should be evaluated through the resulting test's
false-positive rates and power.

Improved MI bias and standard-error estimators could address the sparse-table
failures. Their effects should be assessed separately by changing one
estimate while holding the others fixed, then measuring null rejection,
power and estimated direction. Near independence, the quadratic sampling
approximation may support a more accurate comparison of MI differences.
Any likelihood-ratio or resampling procedure must preserve the equal-MI
null even when the complete population tables differ.

Reversed power paths, stronger dependence at small sample sizes,
additional association constructions, unequal margins and unequal sample
sizes would assess whether power rankings persist across a wider range
of populations. Simulations from plausible application populations could
also examine sensitivity to rare cells and distinct equal-MI tables,
with conclusions tied to the populations chosen for that assessment.

\chapter{Near-Independence Calculations}
\label{app:derivation-details}

These calculations support the near-independence results in
Chapter~\ref{chap:expanded} and their interpretation in
Chapter~\ref{chap:results}. The first calculation varies population
association while keeping the margins fixed. The second retains the
quadratic sampling variation needed at independence and very small MI.

Let \(P_0=(q_{ij})\) be independent, with positive cells
\(q_{ij}=a_i b_j\). Consider \(P_t=P_0+tH\), where every row and column
sum of \(H\) is zero. For sufficiently small \(t\), all cells remain
positive and the margins remain \(a\) and \(b\). We expand around
\(t=0\), where \(I(P_0)=0\).
\par
\end{samepage}

For \(f(t)=I(P_t)\), the second-order Taylor formula is
\begin{equation}
 f(t)=f(0)+f'(0)t+\frac{f''(0)}{2!}t^2+O(t^3).
\end{equation}
Here \(O(t^3)\) collects the omitted terms whose magnitude is bounded by
a constant times \(|t|^3\) as \(t\) approaches zero. These terms become
smaller than the retained quadratic term. The same notation below describes
the size of each omitted remainder near zero.

The row conditional mean also has no first-order term. Its denominator
remains \(a_i\) because the margins are fixed, and
\begin{align*}
 \E_{P_t}\{\pmi_{P_t}(X,Y)\mid X=i\}
 &=\frac{1}{a_i}\sum_j(q_{ij}+tH_{ij})
   \left\{\frac{tH_{ij}}{q_{ij}}+O(t^2)\right\}\\*
 &=\frac{t}{a_i}\sum_jH_{ij}+O(t^2)
 =O(t^2).
\end{align*}
The last equality uses the zero row sum of \(H\). The column mean has the
same cancellation, using \(\sum_iH_{ij}=0\).

In Equation~\eqref{eq:g-final}, the squared centred pointwise MI,
\(V(P_t)\), the conditional means and \(I(P_t)\) all begin at order
\(t^2\). Only the unsquared pointwise-MI term in the bracket has a
first-order contribution. Therefore Equation
\eqref{eq:g-final} supplies the first-order term:
\begin{equation}
 g_{P_t}(i,j)=\frac{2tH_{ij}}{q_{ij}}+O(t^2).
\end{equation}
Since \(g_{P_t}\) has mean zero, its variance is its second moment:
\begin{align}
 \tau^2(P_t)
 &=\sum_{i,j}(q_{ij}+tH_{ij})
   \left\{\frac{2tH_{ij}}{q_{ij}}+O(t^2)\right\}^2\notag\\*
 &=4t^2\sum_{i,j}\frac{H_{ij}^2}{q_{ij}}+O(t^3).
\end{align}
Comparing the leading terms of \(I(P_t)\), \(V(P_t)\) and \(\tau^2(P_t)\)
gives \(V(P_t)\approx2I(P_t)\) and
\(\tau^2(P_t)\approx4V(P_t)\) for small positive MI along this path.
At \(t=0\), the first-order sampling variance is zero;
Appendix~\ref{sec:independence-boundary} treats that case separately.

\section{The independence boundary}
\label{sec:independence-boundary}

At independence, \(p_{ij}=p_{i+}p_{+j}\), so every population
pointwise-MI value is \(\pmi_P(i,j)=\log 1=0\). Consequently,
\(I(P)=V(P)=0\), and the first-order change in MI is zero. Sampling can
still produce positive estimated MI, but its leading variation comes from
second-order cell errors.

For a multinomial sample, take \(\varepsilon h=\widehat P-P\).
Since cell-probability errors typically have size proportional to \(n^{-1/2}\),
squaring them makes \(\Ihat(P)\) proportional to \(n^{-1}\) under
independence. Under fixed table dimensions and positive cell probabilities,
the likelihood-ratio result is
\begin{equation}
 2n\Ihat(P)\xrightarrow{d}\chi^2_{(r-1)(c-1)}
 \label{eq:independence-chi-squared}
\end{equation}
\citep{wilks1938,brillinger2004}. This is the usual one-table likelihood-ratio,
or \(G\), test of independence. Its chi-squared distribution comes from
quadratic cell errors, whereas Normal Wald and Expanded Welch use the
first-order MI error. The two-sample first-order approximation therefore
does not apply unchanged at exact independence.

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{Sampling variation at small positive MI.}

The quadratic approximation also explains why estimated degrees of freedom
remain several units when population MI is almost zero. Keep \(r\) and
\(c\) fixed and let a positive population table approach independence with
cell departures proportional to \(n^{-1/2}\). The normal sampling errors
and the population departure then contribute on the same scale. In regular
models, the likelihood-ratio statistic has a noncentral chi-squared limit
under local alternatives \citep{banerjee2005}. For the multinomial model
here, assume strictly positive limiting cell probabilities. The local
approximation is
\begin{equation}
 G=2n\Ihat(P)\ \dot\sim\ \chi^2_d(\kappa),
 \qquad d=(r-1)(c-1),\qquad \kappa\simeq2nI(P),
 \label{eq:local-noncentral-mi}
\end{equation}
where \(\dot\sim\) denotes an approximate distribution. The noncentral
chi-squared distribution describes a sum of squared normal errors with a
nonzero mean departure; \(\kappa\) measures that departure. At independence,
\(\kappa=0\), recovering Equation~\eqref{eq:independence-chi-squared}.

For the \(4\times4\), \(n=1{,}000\), \(I(P)=0.0001\) setting,
\(d=9\) and \(\kappa\simeq0.2\). The local calculation gives a mean
estimated component degree of freedom of approximately 4.6, rather than
the population first-order value 0.1. It also predicts that the average
plug-in estimate of \(\Var\{\Vhat(P)\}\) divided by its actual sampling
variance is approximately
\begin{equation}
 \frac{4(d+\kappa)/n^2}{2(d+2\kappa)/n^2}
 =\frac{2(d+\kappa)}{d+2\kappa}\simeq1.96.
\end{equation}
This explains the scale of the estimated degrees of freedom and the
roughly twofold plug-in overprediction in Table~\ref{tab:variance-stability}.
The population formula alone omits the quadratic sampling contribution
responsible for both effects.

\section{Copying construction and target selection}

For the copying construction in Equation~\eqref{eq:copying-construction},
summing a row gives
\begin{equation}
 \sum_jp_{ij}(\lambda)
 =(1-\lambda)a_i\sum_ja_j+\lambda a_i=a_i.
\end{equation}
Summing a column similarly gives \(a_j\), so both margins are preserved.

sampled populations use the interior solution. Accept a table only when
every cell is positive, its total and marginal errors are at most
\(10^{-12}\), and its MI error is at most
\(10^{-12}+10^{-8}I_{\rm target}\). Every target is checked against its own population entropy endpoint,
including the alternatives scaled by the fitted null standard deviation.

\section{Validity and sparse-sample measures}
\label{sec:validity-rules}

Normal Wald requires a finite corrected difference, a finite positive
standard error, \(\Vhat(P)+\Vhat(Q)>10^{-14}\), and a finite p-value.
The threshold treats variances extremely close to zero as numerically
unusable. Expanded Welch additionally requires positive finite degrees
of freedom for both components and their combination, and a finite
expanded p-value. A failed component makes Expanded Welch invalid under
this rule.

The primary rate divides valid rejections by all repetitions. A
method-valid rate uses only that method's valid repetitions; a
common-valid rate uses only repetitions where both tests are valid. Report
the denominator for either conditional rate, which is undefined when
the denominator is zero. Invalid outputs contribute no rejection to
the primary rate.

Record the number of zero-count cells, empty rows and empty columns
separately for each population. These are sampling diagnostics rather
than eligibility rules. The minimum expected cell count is
\(\min_{ij}np_{ij}\), with the corresponding definition for \(Q\).
The study applies no minimum expected-count filter.

\section{Bias, variance and degrees of freedom}
\label{sec:estimation-diagnostics}

Let \(\widehat\Delta_s\) be the corrected difference in repetition
\(s\). Its bias estimate is the mean of the finite-valued MI difference
estimates minus the known \(\Delta\). Its observed sampling variance is
\begin{equation}
 \frac{1}{M-1}\sum_{s=1}^M
 \left(\widehat\Delta_s-\frac{1}{M}\sum_{u=1}^M\widehat\Delta_u\right)^2,
 \label{eq:observed-sampling-variance}
\end{equation}
where \(M\) counts the finite-valued differences, including those whose
test output is invalid. Centring at their sample mean separates variance
from bias. For \(P\) and \(Q\), the individual corrected MI biases
are the mean finite corrected MI estimates minus \(I(P)\) and \(I(Q)\),
respectively.

For the estimated / observed variance ratio, restrict the calculations to
the same repetitions with a finite difference and finite squared
standard error. Retain finite zero variance estimates. Divide the mean
squared standard error by the observed variance on this matched subset.
Report the included fraction. The ratio is defined only when the observed
variance is positive. The population comparison instead uses
\(V(P)/n_P+V(Q)/n_Q\) and the primary observed variance.

The Monte Carlo standard error of estimated bias is the observed SD
divided by \(\sqrt M\). Component and combined degrees-of-freedom
summaries retain positive finite values and report their included fractions.
Finite zero variance estimates remain in moment calculations even when
component degrees of freedom are undefined. Percentile ranges describe
sampling spread. Figures divide the mean estimate by its moment target
only where every component estimate is defined; conditional summaries
elsewhere retain their inclusion counts. These diagnostics do not isolate
each estimation error's causal contribution to rejection.

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{Variability of the estimated MI variance.}

For each selected population, measure the observed variability of
\(\Vhat(P)\) by replacing \(\widehat\Delta_s\) with
\(\widehat V_s(P)\) in Equation~\eqref{eq:observed-sampling-variance}.
This measures how much the variance estimate itself changes between
samples. Chapter~\ref{chap:expanded} predicts that variability to first
order. Compare the observed value with
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 \text{population prediction}&=\frac{\tau^2(P)}{n_P},\\
 \text{mean plug-in prediction}&=
 \frac{1}{M}\sum_{s=1}^{M}\frac{\widehat\tau_s^2(P)}{n_P}.
\end{aligned}
 \label{eq:variance-stability-predictions}
\end{equation}
The population prediction uses the known probabilities, whereas the mean plug-in
prediction uses the empirical probabilities in each repetition. Repeat both for
\(Q\). For each population, use the same repetitions with finite
\(\widehat V_s\) and \(\widehat\tau_s^2\), including finite zeros
and outputs whose test is invalid. Divide both predictions by the same
observed variability. A ratio below one indicates underprediction, a ratio
above one indicates overprediction, and one indicates agreement. The
observed variability must be positive; a zero prediction gives a zero ratio.

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{Estimated direction among rejections.}

For a nonzero population difference, classify each valid two-sided rejection
by the sign of \(\Deltahat\). The estimate has the opposite sign when
\(\Deltahat\Delta<0\); it has the correct sign when
\(\Deltahat\Delta>0\). Report the number of rejections and the
number with opposite signs for each method. The fraction with opposite
signs divides the opposite-sign count by the rejection count and is undefined
if there are no rejections. These counts supplement the estimate of power,
which includes every valid rejection regardless of direction.

\section{Simulation uncertainty}
\label{sec:simulation-uncertainty}

For a rate estimate \(\widehat r\) from \(M\) independent repetitions,
its approximate Monte Carlo standard error is
\(\{\widehat r(1-\widehat r)/M\}^{1/2}\).
Rejection and validity rates use pointwise 95\% Wilson intervals
\citep{wilson1927}.

For the paired method contrast, let \(D_s\) equal the Expanded Welch
valid-rejection indicator minus Normal Wald's valid-rejection indicator
in repetition \(s\). The approximate interval for the average paired difference
\(\bar D\) is
\begin{equation}
 \bar D\ \pm\ 1.96
 \left\{\frac{1}{M(M-1)}\sum_{s=1}^M(D_s-\bar D)^2\right\}^{1/2}.
\end{equation}
Use the same common-valid subset when reporting a conditional paired
contrast. Comparisons across constructions or sample allocations use
independent streams and therefore do not use paired indicators. All
intervals describe simulation uncertainty at fixed
populations, not simultaneous coverage over every setting.

\medskip
\thesisminiheading{Estimating the targets and their uncertainty.}

For a component, let \(X_s=\widehat V_s\) in repetition \(s\). Use
all finite values, including zeros, even if component degrees of freedom
are undefined. From \(M\) repetitions, calculate
\begin{equation}
 \bar X=\frac1M\sum_{s=1}^M X_s,\qquad
 S_X^2=\frac1{M-1}\sum_{s=1}^M(X_s-\bar X)^2.
\end{equation}
For \(S_X^2>0\), the estimated moment target is \(2\bar X^2/S_X^2\).
The diagnostic decomposition uses these evaluation moments.

Mean and variance ratios use the same joint delta-method calculation,
keeping the plug-in prediction and observed variance paired. For the
fitted null SD, apply the sampling-variance calculation to the corrected
MI differences and propagate through the square root, whose derivative
at \(S_X^2\) is \(1/(2S_X)\).

\section{Empirical calibration and power uncertainty}
\label{sec:calibration-sensitivity-design}

Calibration follows the fitting and independent evaluation steps in
Chapter~\ref{chap:design}. For Expanded Welch, assign invalid fitting
outputs p-value one and sort the fitting p-values. Set the threshold to
the \((\lfloor0.05M\rfloor+1)\)th smallest value, rejecting only
strictly smaller evaluation p-values. Ties at the boundary are excluded.
Normal Wald uses the equivalent upper-tail threshold for \(|T|\), with
invalid fitting values below all valid absolute statistics. This gives
at most 5\% rejection in the fitting batch; independent null evaluation
measures the achieved rate, including discreteness.

The calibration-sensitivity comparison uses the lower and upper nulls in
Table~\ref{tab:design-calibration-populations} at \(h=2,4\) for A--C.
For each upper null, solve for the copying probability with the original
margin vectors, dimensions and sample sizes. Generate 100,000 independent
fitting repetitions and 100,000 validation repetitions for each of these
six nulls. Apply both calibrations to the same original alternatives and
to both null validation populations. Invalid outputs remain non-rejections.

All calibrated-power intervals use 1,000 joint bootstrap repetitions.
For each full curve, share one lower fitting resample across its points.
For the sensitivity comparison, share one lower fitting resample across
the two alternatives within each focus setting. Independently resample
each upper fitting batch and refit the cutoffs. At each evaluation point,
resample the tests' joint decisions; in the sensitivity comparison, retain
both calibrations in that joint resample. This preserves dependence between
methods and between calibrations when estimating power differences and
changes in those differences. Population tables and effect sizes stay fixed.

Use the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles for pointwise intervals of rates and
paired differences, comparing the latter with the practical tolerance of
minus one to plus one percentage point. Cross-null rates use Wilson
intervals conditional on the fitted cutoffs, quantifying validation
sampling uncertainty only. These checks concern the two specified null
populations.
